title: Ghazals of longing
hook: his Persian love-poems to the Divine are still sung in gurdwaras

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zindagi Nama, and your line, see him everywhere. What ordinary thing did you look at with longing? Day seven hundred fifteen.

In a gurdwara, the ragis sit with harmonium and tabla, and sing the Guru's own word from the Guru Granth Sahib. Then, now and then, the words change color. The language turns Persian. The tune softens. And the song is a love song, sung to God, by someone who sounds as if he can hardly bear the distance. Those songs were written by the poet we met two days ago. Today's word: ghazal.
screen: `RAGIS, HARMONIUM, TABLA.` → `THE WORDS CHANGE COLOR.` → `A LOVE SONG, SUNG TO GOD.`

segments.voice: A ghazal is a love poem with a shape of its own. The form began in Arabic and flowered in Persian. It's built from couplets, pairs of lines, and each couplet is complete in itself, like a bead. String the beads together and you have the ghazal. By custom, the poet signs the poem near the end, slipping his pen name into the last couplet. So in Bhai Nand Lal's ghazals, you'll hear him name himself: Goya. His ghazals are gathered in a collection known as the Divan-e-Goya. And what are they about? Longing. The lover and the Beloved. The ache of distance, the sweetness of a glance, the lover who would give anything for one meeting. That's the old language of the Persian ghazal, and Nand Lal draws on it. But in his poems the Beloved is the Divine, and the face the heart turns toward is the One, seen through the Guru. Hold three things together. First, the form. Each couplet stands alone, so a ragi can sing one, or several, and each still makes sense. A ghazal is easy to carry in pieces. Second, the feeling. Some people picture devotion as duty, a list of things to do. Nand Lal's ghazals sound more like someone who's simply in love, and can't hide it. Third, the place. These Persian love-songs aren't kept on a library shelf. They're sung in gurdwaras, in kirtan, in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib. Sikh custom welcomes them there. So a Persian love form found a home in the Guru's house, and it came in singing about love.
screen: `COUPLETS, EACH COMPLETE.` · `THE POET SIGNS: GOYA.` · `THE BELOVED IS THE DIVINE.` · `SUNG IN THE GURDWARA.` · then, large: `LOVE, IN PERSIAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one ghazal. If you can, find a recording of a ghazal of Bhai Nand Lal sung in kirtan, and play just a few minutes of it during the sit. If you can't, sit with the idea of one: a single couplet, complete in itself, sung slowly to someone you love. Don't try to understand every word. Let the sound do its work. Notice where the music lifts, and where it waits. If you pray, you can let Waheguru rise in you along with the tune. The bell holds the time.
Ghazal. A love poem built from couplets, as Persian poets shaped it, signed with the poet's pen name. Bhai Nand Lal's ghazals, signed Goya, are love songs to the Divine.
Your line: love, in persian. Today, hum one line of a song you love as if it were addressed to the One, and notice how it changes. Day seven hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Ragis sing Bhai Nand Lal's Persian ghazals in kirtan in gurdwaras, alongside the Guru's bani, and Sikhs also read them in Persian and in translation.

what a scholar hears: Nand Lal keeps the ghazal's lover's language and makes the Beloved the Divine, seen through the Guru.
